plain_english: You'll notice that the most powerful and important people often say they wish they had more free time. They praise it and say they'd rather have leisure than all the privileges they currently enjoy. Sometimes they want to step down from their high positions — if only they could do it safely. But power often destroys itself under its own weight, even without any outside attack.
original_excerpt: You will find that the most powerful and highly-placed men let fall phrases in which they long for leisure, praise it, and prefer it to all the blessings which they enjoy. Sometimes they would fain descend from their lofty pedestal, if it could be safely done: for Fortune collapses by its own weight, without any shock or interference from without.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 4

plain_english: Even Emperor Augustus — who received more gifts from the gods than anyone else — never stopped hoping for rest and a break from running the empire. He would comfort himself during his long work days with a sweet but impossible dream: that someday he would live only for himself. In a letter to the Senate, he promised that his retirement would still be dignified and wouldn't dishonor his past achievements. Then he wrote: "It's better to actually do these things than just promise them. But I'm so eager for that time I long for that I get pleasure just from talking about it, even though it's still far away." He valued free time so much that even though he couldn't have it, he enjoyed it by imagining it and thinking about it.
original_excerpt: The late Emperor Augustus, upon whom the gods bestowed more blessings than on any one else, never ceased to pray for rest and exemption from the troubles of empire: he used to enliven his labours with this sweet, though unreal consolation, that he would some day live for himself alone. In a letter which he addressed to the Senate, after promising that his rest shall not be devoid of dignity nor discreditable to his former glories, I find the following words:—"These things, however, it is more honourable to do than to promise: but my eagerness for that time, so earnestly longed for, has led me to derive a certain pleasure from speaking about it, though the reality is still far distant." He thought leisure so important, that though he could not actually enjoy it, yet he did so by anticipation and by thinking about it.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 4

plain_english: This man saw that everything depended on him alone. He controlled the fate of individuals and entire nations. Yet he thought his happiest day would be when he finally gave up all that power. He knew from experience how much work went into maintaining that glory that stretched across the world. He knew how much hidden worry came with it. He had been forced to fight wars to defend his position — first against his own countrymen, then against his colleagues, and finally against his own family. He had spilled blood on both sea and land. He had marched his armies through Macedonia, Sicily, Egypt, Syria, Asia Minor, and almost every country in the world. When his troops were tired of killing Romans, he turned them against foreign enemies instead.
original_excerpt: He, who saw everything depending upon himself alone, who swayed the fortunes of men and of nations, thought that his happiest day would be that on which he laid aside his greatness. He knew by experience how much labour was involved in that glory that shone through all lands, and how much secret anxiety was concealed within it: he had been forced to assert his rights by war, first with his countrymen, next with his colleagues, and lastly with his own relations, and had shed blood both by sea and by land: after marching his troops under arms through Macedonia, Sicily, Egypt, Syria, Asia Minor, and almost all the countries of the world, when they were weary with slaughtering Romans he had directed them against a foreign foe.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 4

plain_english: While Augustus was conquering the Alpine regions and defeating enemies within the Roman empire itself, while he was pushing the borders beyond the Rhine, Euphrates, and Danube rivers, back in Rome conspirators like Murena, Caepio, Lepidus, Egnatius, and others were sharpening their swords to kill him. He barely escaped their plot when his failing health was shaken by his own daughter's scandal — she had slept with young nobles who swore loyalty to her through adultery. Then came the threat of Paulus and Mark Antony's mistress, dangerous to Rome once again. When he cut out these infected parts of his body, new ones grew back. The empire was like a body with too much blood — always bursting somewhere. That's why he craved peace and quiet. All his hard work was driven by the hope of someday having leisure. The man who could grant everyone else's wishes had this one wish for himself.
original_excerpt: While he was pacifying the Alpine regions, and subduing the enemies whom he found in the midst of the Roman empire, while he was extending its boundaries beyond the Rhine, the Euphrates, and the Danube, at Rome itself the swords of Murena, Caepio, Lepidus, Egnatius, and others were being sharpened to slay him. Scarcely had he escaped from their plot, when his already failing age was terrified by his daughter and all the noble youths who were pledged to her cause by adultery with her by way of oath of fidelity. Then there was Paulus and Antonius's mistress, a second time to be feared by Rome: and when he had cut out these ulcers from his very limbs, others grew in their place: the empire, like a body overloaded with blood, was always breaking out somewhere. For this reason he longed for leisure: all his labours were based upon hopes and thoughts of leisure: this was the wish of him who could accomplish the wishes of all other men.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 4
